chunks: Ibn al-Walid, from al-Saffar, from al-Yaqtini, from Ibn Abi Najran who said:

I asked Aba Ja’far the Second (peace be upon him) about Tawhid, saying: Should I imagine a thing? He said: Yes, (something) neither cognizable nor delimited. Whatever your imagination falls upon is different than He. Nothing is like Him and imaginations do not reach Him. How can imaginations reach Him when He is other than what can be cognized and other than what is represented in the imaginations? It is imagined something neither cognizable nor delimited.
ai.seo_question: How should one conceive of God's nature if He cannot be fully understood or limited?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) articulates the Shia doctrine of *Tawhid al-Sifat* (Unity of Attributes), emphasizing that divine essence transcends all human conceptualization. It establishes that any mental image or attribute we ascribe to God is necessarily a negation of His true nature, as He is 'not limited' and 'not comprehensible' to the intellect. This serves as a safeguard against anthropomorphism (*Tashbih*) and excessive speculation (*Ta'til*), affirming that God is unlike anything in creation.

en.ammaar-muslim: 9. [9/378] al-Tawhid: Ibn al-Walid from al-Saffar from al-Yaqtini from Ibn Abi Najran who said:

I asked Aba Ja’far the Second عليه السلام about Tawhid saying: Should I imagine a thing (when conceiving of God)? He said: Yes, (something) neither cognizable nor delimited. Whatever your imagination falls upon is different than He. Nothing is like Him and imaginations do not reach Him. How can imaginations reach Him when He is other than what can be cognized and other than what is represented (images formed) in the imaginations? It is imagined something neither cognizable nor delimited.
